chapterTitle: Armed with Christ's Mind in the Fiery Trial
themeTitle: “Don’t Be Astonished at the Fiery Trial”

scripture.text: Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind; for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin;
scripture.understanding: Χριστοῦ οὖν παθόντος σαρκί, “Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh” — πάσχω, from the suffer family, picking up 3:18. καὶ ὑμεῖς τὴν αὐτὴν ἔννοιαν ὁπλίσασθε, “arm yourselves also with the same mind” — ὁπλίζω, to put on armour, a soldier's word; ἔννοια, a settled way of thinking, a resolve. ὅτι ὁ παθὼν σαρκὶ πέπαυται ἁμαρτίας, “for he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin” — the one who has accepted suffering for Christ has broken with sin's rule; he has chosen God's will over comfort (Romans 6:7). ἁμαρτία, from the sin family.

scripture.text: that you no longer should live the rest of your time in the flesh for the lusts of men, but for the will of God.
scripture.understanding: εἰς τὸ μηκέτι ἀνθρώπων ἐπιθυμίαις ἀλλὰ θελήματι θεοῦ τὸν ἐπίλοιπον ἐν σαρκὶ βιῶσαι χρόνον, “that you no longer should live the rest of your time in the flesh for the lusts of men, but for the will of God” — βιόω, from the life family: to live out the course of an earthly life (βίος), as distinct from ζάω, simply to be alive. χρόνος, from the time family: the span of time left. The rest of your life has two possible masters: human desires (ἐπιθυμία) or God's θέλημα.

scripture.text: For we have spent enough of our past time doing the desire of the Gentiles, and having walked in lewdness, lusts, drunken binges, orgies, carousings, and abominable idolatries.
scripture.understanding: ἀρκετὸς γὰρ ὁ παρεληλυθὼς χρόνος, “For we have spent enough of our past time” — ἀρκετός, sufficient: the past was more than enough. χρόνος again, from the time family. τὸ βούλημα τῶν ἐθνῶν κατειργάσθαι, “doing the desire of the Gentiles” — βούλημα, what the pagan world wants; κατεργάζομαι, from the work family: to carry out fully. Then a list of pagan festival life: ἀσέλγεια, “lewdness” — shameless sensuality; ἐπιθυμία, “lusts”; οἰνοφλυγία, “drunken binges”; κῶμος, “orgies” — wild night processions; πότος, “carousings” — drinking parties; ἀθέμιτοι εἰδωλολατρίαι, “abominable idolatries” — forbidden worship. This was the readers' own former life.

scripture.text: They think it is strange that you don’t run with them into the same excess of riot, blaspheming:
scripture.understanding: ἐν ᾧ ξενίζονται, “They think it is strange” — ξενίζω, to find something foreign, surprising; the same verb appears in verse 12. μὴ συντρεχόντων ὑμῶν, “that you don’t run with them” — συντρέχω, to run together like a crowd in a stampede. εἰς τὴν αὐτὴν τῆς ἀσωτίας ἀνάχυσιν, “into the same excess of riot” — ἀνάχυσις, an overflowing flood; ἀσωτία, reckless waste, the word for the prodigal son's ‘riotous living’. βλασφημοῦντες, “blaspheming” — they slander the believers and, through them, God.

scripture.text: who will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.
scripture.understanding: οἳ ἀποδώσουσιν λόγον, “who will give account” — λόγος, from the word family, here a reckoning, an account rendered. τῷ ἑτοίμως ἔχοντι κρῖναι ζῶντας καὶ νεκρούς, “to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead” — ἑτοίμως, ready now; ζάω, from the life family. The scoffers will answer to Christ, the Judge (Acts 10:42). κρίνω is from the judge family — to judge — to decide, try, condemn or vindicate.

scripture.text: For to this end the Good News was preached even to the dead, that they might be judged indeed as men in the flesh, but live as to God in the spirit.
scripture.understanding: εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ νεκροῖς εὐηγγελίσθη, “For to this end the Good News was preached even to the dead” — εὐαγγελίζω. The strongest reading, following verse 5, is that the gospel was preached to people while they were alive who have since died: believers who were mocked and judged by people, and then died — as their pagan neighbours said, ‘What good did their faith do them?’ ἵνα κριθῶσι μὲν κατὰ ἀνθρώπους σαρκί, “that they might be judged indeed as men in the flesh” — condemned by human verdict, and they died like everyone else. ζῶσι δὲ κατὰ θεὸν πνεύματι, “but live as to God in the spirit” — ζάω, from the life family: alive to God. It is not a second chance after death, which Scripture never offers. κρίνω is from the judge family — to judge — to decide, try, condemn or vindicate.

scripture.text: But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer.
scripture.understanding: πάντων δὲ τὸ τέλος ἤγγικεν, “But the end of all things is near” — τέλος, from the perfect family: the goal, the end towards which history is moving; ἐγγίζω, the ‘at hand’ of James 5:8. σωφρονήσατε οὖν καὶ νήψατε εἰς προσευχάς, “Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer” — two words from the self-control family: σωφρονέω, to keep a sound, balanced mind, and νήφω, to be sober, clear-headed, free from every kind of intoxication. προσευχή, from the pray family. The nearness of the end does not call for panic or speculation but for clear-headed prayer.

scripture.text: And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.
scripture.understanding: πρὸ πάντων, ‘above all things’ — the very phrase James used before his warning about oaths (James 5:12). τὴν εἰς ἑαυτοὺς ἀγάπην ἐκτενῆ ἔχοντες, “be earnest in your love among yourselves” — ἀγάπη, from the love family; ἐκτενής, stretched out, at full strength, as in 1:22. ὅτι ἀγάπη καλύπτει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν, “for love covers a multitude of sins” — from Proverbs 10:12, the same proverb James used in his last verse (James 5:20). καλύπτω, to cover: love does not expose and broadcast others' sins but forgives, forbears and restores. ἁμαρτία, from the sin family.

scripture.text: Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
scripture.understanding: φιλόξενοι εἰς ἀλλήλους, “Be hospitable to one another” — φιλόξενος, from the love family: a lover of strangers, the quality required of overseers (Titus 1:8). Travelling believers and the poor depended on open homes. ἄνευ γογγυσμοῦ, “without grumbling” — γογγυσμός, muttering under the breath. Hospitality given with complaint ruins the gift.

scripture.text: As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.
scripture.understanding: ἕκαστος καθὼς ἔλαβεν χάρισμα, “As each has received a gift” — χάρισμα, from the gift family: a gift of grace, every believer has at least one. εἰς ἑαυτοὺς αὐτὸ διακονοῦντες, “employ it in serving one another” — διακονέω, from the servant family: to wait on others. ὡς καλοὶ οἰκονόμοι ποικίλης χάριτος θεοῦ, “as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms” — οἰκονόμος, also from the servant family: a household steward who manages what belongs to the master; καλός, from the good family; ποικίλος, many-coloured, the ‘various’ trials of 1:6 — God's grace comes in as many colours as our troubles.

scripture.text: If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
scripture.understanding: εἴ τις λαλεῖ, ὡς λόγια θεοῦ, “If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God” — λόγιον, from the word family: an oracle, a divine utterance (Romans 3:2). Speakers must handle their words as God's, not their own. εἴ τις διακονεῖ (διακονέω, from the servant family, as in v. 10), ὡς ἐξ ἰσχύος ἧς χορηγεῖ ὁ θεός, “If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies” — ἰσχύς, from the power family: inherent strength, might; χορηγέω, to supply generously, originally to pay for a chorus. Then a doxology with two power-family words: ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος, “the glory and the dominion” — κράτος, ruling might, power that prevails, as distinct from ἰσχύς, the strength God supplies for service. αἰῶνας, in the time family and the world family: ‘forever and ever’, the ages upon ages.

scripture.text: Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you, to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you.
scripture.understanding: ἀγαπητοί, “Beloved” — from the love family. μὴ ξενίζεσθε τῇ ἐν ὑμῖν πυρώσει, “don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you” — ξενίζω, to treat something as foreign; πύρωσις, a burning, the refiner's fire (Proverbs 27:21), recalling the gold tested by fire (1:7). πρὸς πειρασμὸν ὑμῖν γινομένῃ, “to test you” — πειρασμός, from the test family. ὡς ξένου ὑμῖν συμβαίνοντος, “as though a strange thing happened to you” — ξένος, foreign. Suffering is not an alien intrusion into the Christian life; it is the normal path of those who follow Christ.

scripture.text: But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice; that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy.
scripture.understanding: ἀλλὰ καθὸ κοινωνεῖτε τοῖς τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθήμασιν, χαίρετε, “But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice” — κοινωνέω, to share, to have fellowship in; πάθημα, from the suffer family. Paul longed for ‘the fellowship of his sufferings’ (Philippians 3:10). ἵνα καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀποκαλύψει τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ χαρῆτε ἀγαλλιώμενοι, “that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy” — ἀποκάλυψις, from the appear family; ἀγαλλιάω, leaping joy, as in 1:6, 8. Joy now in fellowship, joy then in glory.

scripture.text: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed; because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you. On their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified.
scripture.understanding: εἰ ὀνειδίζεσθε ἐν ὀνόματι Χριστοῦ, μακάριοι, “If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed” — ὀνειδίζω, to reproach, the word James used for God not ‘reproaching’ those who ask (James 1:5); Jesus used it in the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:11). ὅτι τὸ τῆς δόξης καὶ τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεῦμα ἐφ᾽ ὑμᾶς ἀναπαύεται, “because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you” — ἀναπαύω, from the rest family: to settle and remain, as the Spirit rested on the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2) and the glory rested on the tabernacle. The last sentence, ‘On their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified’, is found in later manuscripts the WEB follows.

scripture.text: For let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or an evil doer, or a meddler in other men’s matters.
scripture.understanding: μὴ γάρ τις ὑμῶν πασχέτω, “For let none of you suffer” — πάσχω, from the suffer family. Not all suffering is for Christ. ὡς φονεὺς ἢ κλέπτης ἢ κακοποιός, “as a murderer, or a thief, or an evil doer” — κακοποιός, from the evil family, the charge of 2:12 and 3:16, which must never be true. ἢ ὡς ἀλλοτριεπίσκοπος, “or a meddler in other men’s matters” — a rare word, perhaps coined: ‘an overseer of other people's business’, a busybody. Peter puts meddling beside murder: interfering in what is not your business brings deserved trouble.

scripture.text: But if one of you suffers for being a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God in this matter.
scripture.understanding: εἰ δὲ ὡς Χριστιανός, “But if one of you suffers for being a Christian” — Χριστιανός, ‘a Christ-person’, a name first given at Antioch (Acts 11:26), probably by outsiders as a label; it appears only three times in the New Testament (Acts 26:28). μὴ αἰσχυνέσθω, “let him not be ashamed” — αἰσχύνομαι. δοξαζέτω δὲ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ μέρει τούτῳ, “but let him glorify God in this matter” — the earliest manuscripts read ‘in this name’. What the world uses as an insult, the believer wears as an honour.

scripture.text: For the time has come for judgment to begin with the household of God. If it begins first with us, what will happen to those who don’t obey the Good News of God?
scripture.understanding: ὅτι ὁ καιρὸς τοῦ ἄρξασθαι τὸ κρίμα ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴκου τοῦ θεοῦ, “For the time has come for judgment to begin with the household of God” — καιρός, from the time family: the appointed moment, as distinct from χρόνος, the span of time (vv. 2–3). κρίμα, judgement; οἶκος, the house — the ‘spiritual house’ of 2:5. God's refining judgement begins with His own people (Ezekiel 9:6; Malachi 3:1–3). “If it begins first with us, what will happen to those who don’t obey the Good News of God?” — ἀπειθέω, refusing to be persuaded; εὐαγγέλιον. κρίμα is from the judge family — judgement as the verdict or sentence passed.

scripture.text: “If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will happen to the ungodly and the sinner?”
scripture.understanding: Peter quotes Proverbs 11:31 in the Greek Old Testament: “If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will happen to the ungodly and the sinner?” — μόλις, with difficulty, through many trials; σῴζω, from the heal family: rescued, made whole; ἀσεβής, from the godliness family: the irreverent, the ungodly; ἁμαρτωλός, from the sin family. ποῦ φανεῖται, literally ‘where will he appear?’ — φαίνω, from the appear family: where will he stand on that day? Salvation is certain but not easy; for those outside it, the end is unthinkable.

scripture.text: Therefore let them also who suffer according to the will of God in doing good entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator.
scripture.understanding: ὥστε καὶ οἱ πάσχοντες κατὰ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, “Therefore let them also who suffer according to the will of God” — πάσχω, from the suffer family; θέλημα, as in 3:17. ἐν ἀγαθοποιΐᾳ, “in doing good” — ἀγαθοποιΐα, from the good family: keep on doing good while you suffer. πιστῷ κτίστῃ παρατιθέσθωσαν τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν, “entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator” — παρατίθημι, to deposit something for safekeeping, the very word Jesus used on the cross: ‘Father, into your hands I commit my spirit’ (Luke 23:46). ψυχή, from the life family. κτίστης, Creator — only here in the New Testament: the One who made you can keep you.

visualMeditations.title: Putting On the Armour
visualMeditations.image: Picture a soldier in the early morning, strapping on his breastplate, buckling his sword, fixing his helmet. He knows the battle ahead will be painful. He has already decided he will not run. His mind is made up before the trumpet sounds.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind” (v. 1). The weapon Peter gives is not a sword but a mindset — Christ's resolve to do the Father's will whatever it costs. If you decide in advance that obedience matters more than comfort, temptation loses much of its grip, and you can live “the rest of your time in the flesh … for the will of God” (v. 2).

visualMeditations.title: The Party You Left
visualMeditations.image: Picture a group of old friends heading out on a Friday night for drink, noise and whatever happens next. They knock on your door as they always used to. You smile and say you are not coming. They stare at you, puzzled, then laugh and start mocking — ‘What happened to you? Have you become a saint?’ — as they walk off into the night.
visualMeditations.meaning: “They think it is strange that you don’t run with them into the same excess of riot, blaspheming” (v. 4). Peter says the past has had more than enough of our time (v. 3). Their mockery is not the last word: they “will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead” (v. 5). You are not missing out; you have been set free.

visualMeditations.title: The Many-Coloured Grace
visualMeditations.image: Picture a household where the master has left on a long journey. He has given each steward a different store: one has keys to the granary, another the wine cellar, another the guest rooms, another the money chest. When guests arrive, the stewards work together — one cooks, one serves, one prepares the beds — and the house hums with welcome. None of the goods are theirs; all are the master's.
visualMeditations.meaning: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms” (v. 10). Your gift is not your property; it is a store of the Master's grace entrusted to you for others. Speak as if speaking God's words; serve in the strength He supplies, “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (v. 11).

visualMeditations.title: The Fiery Trial
visualMeditations.image: Picture a believer arrested in a Roman city, dragged before a jeering crowd, and mocked for the name ‘Christian’. Flames from a nearby fire light up the faces of the crowd. Yet the believer's face is calm, almost radiant — as if a glory unseen by the crowd is resting on him.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you, to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you” (v. 12). “But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice” (v. 13). “If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed; because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you” (v. 14). In the fire you are never alone; His glory rests on you.

structure.label: Armed with Christ's Mind (v. 1-6)
structure.body: Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same resolve, living the rest of your time for God's will, not human desires; the past was enough for pagan excess, and those who mock you for not joining them will give account to the Judge of the living and the dead; the gospel was preached to those now dead so that, though judged by people, they live to God.

structure.label: Living in View of the End (v. 7-11)
structure.body: The end of all things is near, so be clear-minded and sober for prayer; above all keep love constant, for love covers many sins; be hospitable without grumbling; use every gift to serve others as stewards of God's varied grace, speaking as God's words and serving in His strength, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ.

structure.label: Suffering as a Christian (v. 12-19)
structure.body: Do not be surprised by the fiery trial; rejoice as you share Christ's sufferings, for you will rejoice at His glory; if insulted for Christ's name you are blessed, for the Spirit of glory rests on you; do not suffer as a wrongdoer, but if as a Christian, do not be ashamed but glorify God; judgement begins with God's household; so let those who suffer by God's will entrust themselves to their faithful Creator while doing good.

sections.heading: A Settled Mind and a Clean Break
paragraphs: Chapter 3 ended with Christ's suffering and victory. Chapter 4 draws the conclusion: “Therefore, since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind” (v. 1). The Christian life is warfare, and the first weapon is a decision. Christ resolved to do His Father's will even when it led to the cross. When believers adopt that same resolve, they have made a clean break with sin's rule; the rest of their life is for God's will, not human desires (v. 2). Paul says, “For he who has died has been freed from sin” (Romans 6:7).

That decision makes believers look strange. Peter's readers had once joined in the drinking, sexual excess and idol feasts of their towns (v. 3). Now they stay home, and their old friends are both puzzled and offended: “They think it is strange that you don’t run with them into the same excess of riot, blaspheming” (v. 4). The ridicule hurts, but Peter reminds them who has the final word: their mockers “will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead” (v. 5).

Verse 6 answers a painful question. If faith in Christ does not stop believers from dying, what good is it? Peter says the gospel was preached to those who have now died, so that although they were judged by human standards in the flesh — mocked and buried like everyone else — they live to God in the spirit. This is not a second chance after death, which Scripture never teaches; it is the assurance that believers who die are alive to God.

sections.heading: Love, Hospitality and Gifts at the End of the Age
paragraphs: “But the end of all things is near” (v. 7). The New Testament writers lived with a strong sense that Christ's return could be soon. Peter's response is not panic, date-setting or withdrawal, but sober prayer: “Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer.” Jesus said the same: “Watch therefore, for you don’t know in what hour your Lord comes” (Matthew 24:42). Paul: “The night is far gone, and the day is near” (Romans 13:12).

Above all, believers must keep loving one another at full stretch, “for love covers a multitude of sins” (v. 8). Peter, who had been forgiven a great deal, knew what it was to have sins covered rather than exposed. Love shows itself in open homes — “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (v. 9) — and in using every gift for others.

Every believer has received a χάρισμα, a gift of grace (v. 10). The gifts vary, like God's grace itself, which Peter calls ποικίλη, many-coloured. Paul says, “Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:4). Peter divides them into two broad kinds: speaking gifts and serving gifts. Speakers must speak “as it were the very words of God”; servers must serve “as of the strength which God supplies” (v. 11). The goal is not the fame of the gifted but the glory of God: “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.”

sections.heading: The Fiery Trial and the Faithful Creator
paragraphs: Peter now speaks directly about the persecution his readers are facing. “Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you, to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you” (v. 12). Suffering for Christ is not a sign that something has gone wrong; it is part of following a crucified Lord. In fact, it is cause for joy: “But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice; that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy” (v. 13). The apostles had learned this early: after being flogged, they left the council “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name” (Acts 5:41).

Peter adds a precious promise: “If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed; because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you” (v. 14). As God's glory once rested on the tabernacle, the Spirit of glory rests on suffering believers. But Peter is honest: not all suffering is holy. Believers must never suffer for murder, theft, wrongdoing — or meddling in other people's business (v. 15). But “if one of you suffers for being a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God in this matter” (v. 16).

Then a sobering perspective: “For the time has come for judgment to begin with the household of God” (v. 17). Suffering is God's refining judgement on His own house, purifying it. If even believers are saved only through such trials, “what will happen to the ungodly and the sinner?” (v. 18). The chapter ends with the believer's response: “Therefore let them also who suffer according to the will of God in doing good entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator” (v. 19). The word ‘entrust’ is the word Jesus used on the cross: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). In suffering, do what Jesus did — keep doing good, and place yourself in your Father's hands.

ntConnection.heading: Sharing His Sufferings, Sharing His Glory
paragraphs: Peter's call to rejoice in suffering comes straight from Jesus: “Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Matthew 5:11), “Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven” (Matthew 5:12). Paul expresses the same longing: “that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings” (Philippians 3:10), and he promises, “if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him” (Romans 8:17).

The name ‘Christian’ appears only three times in the New Testament. “The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch” (Acts 11:26). King Agrippa used it with a sneer: “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?” (Acts 26:28). And Peter tells believers not to be ashamed of it (v. 16). What began as a nickname became a badge of honour.

The command to use gifts as stewards echoes Paul's teaching: “Having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us” (Romans 12:6), and his call to hospitality: “contributing to the needs of the saints; given to hospitality” (Romans 12:13). And the closing image — entrusting the soul to a faithful Creator — takes us to Calvary, where Jesus, “crying with a loud voice, said, ‘Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!’” (Luke 23:46).

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “to equip (with weapons (middle voice and figuratively)).” ὁπλίζω comes from ὅπλον, a weapon or piece of armour. Peter uses it only here: the believer's armour is a mind (ἔννοια) — a settled resolve — like Christ's. Paul speaks of ‘the armor of light’ (Romans 13:12) and ‘the whole armor of God’ (Ephesians 6:11). Peter's point is that suffering is easier to bear when the decision to obey has already been made. A mind armed in advance does not surrender at the first blow.

Strong's: “a (divine) gratuity, i.e. deliverance (from danger or passion); (specially), a (spiritual) endowment, i.e. (subjectively) religious qualification, or (objectively) miraculous faculty.” χάρισμα comes from χάρις, grace: a gift of grace. It belongs to the gift family. Peter pairs it with οἰκονόμος, from the servant family: a household manager who handles the master's goods. Your abilities, opportunities and spiritual gifts are not trophies but stewardships, to be used for others and accounted for.

Strong's: “ignition, i.e. (specially), smelting (figuratively, conflagration, calamity as a test).” πύρωσις is a burning, used of the furnace in which metal is refined (Proverbs 27:21). Peter links it to the gold tested by fire in 1:7. The word ‘strange’ (ξένος) and the verb ‘be astonished’ (ξενίζω) come from the same root: suffering is not a foreigner who has wandered into the Christian life. It is a familiar part of the road. The fire refines; it does not destroy.

Strong's: “a Christian, i.e. follower of Christ.” The ending -ιανός marked someone as a partisan or follower of a person, like ‘Herodians’. The name was first given at Antioch (Acts 11:26), probably by outsiders, and used mockingly by Agrippa (Acts 26:28). By Peter's time it could be a criminal charge: Roman writers soon record Christians being punished simply for the name. Peter turns the insult into an honour: to suffer as a ‘Christ-one’ is to glorify God.

Strong's: “to place alongside, i.e. present (food, truth); by implication, to deposit (as a trust or for protection).” παρατίθημι was used of depositing money with a trusted person for safekeeping. Jesus used it with His last breath: ‘Father, into your hands I commit my spirit’ (Luke 23:46). Peter tells suffering believers to do the same with their souls — to deposit them with God, the faithful κτίστης, the Creator. The One who made you is able and faithful to keep what you entrust to Him.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: In this chapter the Holy Spirit is preparing you for opposition, sharpening your love, and teaching you how to entrust yourself to God in the fire.

items.title: Is Your Mind Armed?
items.body: The Spirit asks whether you have settled in advance that you will obey God whatever it costs, or whether you decide again every time temptation or pressure comes. “arm yourselves also with the same mind” (v. 1). What would change this week if you went into each day already resolved to do God's will rather than your own desires?

items.title: What Gift Are You Hoarding?
items.body: You have received a gift of grace — perhaps teaching, encouraging, giving, organising, hospitality, prayer, practical help. The Spirit asks: are you using it to serve others, or keeping it to yourself? “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another” (v. 10). Name your gift and one person who needs it this week.

items.title: Into Whose Hands?
items.body: If you are in a fiery trial now, the Spirit wants you to know it is not strange, and that His glory rests on you (vv. 12–14). He invites you to do what Jesus did: “entrust their souls to him, as to a faithful Creator” (v. 19). Speak it aloud today: ‘Father, into Your hands I commit my spirit — and this situation.’ Then keep doing good.

audit.title: The Old-Life Check
audit.body: Is there anything from your ‘past time’ (v. 3) — habits, places, friendships, entertainment — that is still pulling you back? Are you embarrassed when others think your new life is strange (v. 4)?

audit.title: The Love Check
audit.body: Do you cover others' sins with love, or expose and repeat them (v. 8)? When did you last open your home without grumbling (v. 9)?

audit.title: The Suffering Check
audit.body: When you suffer, is it for being a Christian, or for wrongdoing, foolishness or meddling (vv. 15–16)? Are you ashamed of the name of Christ anywhere in your life?

practices.title: Employ Your Gift This Week
practices.body: Write down what you believe your main gift of grace is (v. 10). Then plan one specific way to use it this week to serve someone in your church — a meal, a visit, a word of encouragement, a practical task, teaching a child, praying with someone. Do it as a steward, not an owner, and ask God for His strength (v. 11).

practices.title: The Entrusting Prayer
practices.body: Each evening this week, before you sleep, take your current trial or worry and pray the words of Luke 23:46 and 1 Peter 4:19: ‘Father, into Your hands I entrust my soul and this situation. You are my faithful Creator.’ Then write down one good thing you will do tomorrow despite the pressure.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, You suffered in the flesh for me. Arm me with Your mind, so that I live the rest of my time not for human desires but for the will of God. The past has had more than enough of my life; I will not run back into the flood of excess, even when others find it strange and speak evil of me. I know they will give account to You, the Judge of the living and the dead. The end of all things is near, so keep me clear-minded and sober for prayer. Above all, stretch my love to full strength, because love covers a multitude of sins. Make my home open and my heart free from grumbling. Thank You for the gift of grace You have given me; help me use it to serve others as a good steward of Your many-coloured grace — speaking as Your words and serving in the strength You supply, so that You are glorified in everything. When the fiery trial comes, let me not be astonished. Let me rejoice to share in Your sufferings, knowing I will rejoice at the revelation of Your glory. If I am insulted for Your name, let me know that the Spirit of glory rests on me. Let me never suffer for wrongdoing, and never be ashamed to be called a Christian. Like You on the cross, I entrust my soul to my faithful Creator, and I will keep on doing good. In Your name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: The Apostles Rejoice After Flogging
storyConnections.summary: The high priest had Peter and the apostles arrested for preaching about Jesus. An angel released them, and they went straight back to teaching in the temple. Brought before the council again, Peter declared that they must obey God rather than men. The council had them flogged and ordered them not to speak in Jesus' name. “They therefore departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name” (Acts 5:41). Peter writes chapter 4 as a man who had felt the whip and found joy in it.

storyConnections.title: Stephen Entrusts His Spirit
storyConnections.summary: Stephen, full of grace and power, was falsely accused before the council. As he spoke, all who sat in the council saw his face like the face of an angel. When he finished, they rushed at him, dragged him out of the city and stoned him. Looking up, he saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. As the stones fell he prayed, ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!’ and, kneeling, ‘Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!’ He is a picture of verse 14 — the Spirit of glory resting on a believer insulted for Christ — and verse 19, entrusting his soul to God while doing good to his enemies.

storyConnections.title: Jesus Commits His Spirit to the Father
storyConnections.summary: At noon darkness covered the land until three in the afternoon, and the curtain of the temple was torn in two. Then Jesus, “crying with a loud voice, said, ‘Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!’ Having said this, he breathed his last” (Luke 23:46). The verb ‘commit’ is the same verb Peter uses in verse 19, ‘entrust’. Jesus did not entrust Himself to the crowd, the governor or His friends, but to His Father, the faithful Creator. He suffered in the flesh (v. 1) and handed Himself to God. Peter tells every suffering believer to follow those steps.
